real_s2.explanation: The unit responds to a dog's face seen straight on and looking directly at the camera, most strongly when the face is large in the frame. Activity drops when the head is turned or in profile, when the face is small, or when no face is visible.

parsed.explanation: The unit responds to a dog's face seen straight on and looking directly at the camera, most strongly when the face is large in the frame. Activity drops when the head is turned or in profile, when the face is small, or when no face is visible.
parsed.evidence: All three gaze and pose predictions held after removing class differences: direct gaze vs. no face d +1.64 (98th percentile), frontal vs. profile d +1.24 (97th), large vs. small face d +1.20 (95th). Dog count did not matter (d +0.35, 73rd percentile), so the unit tracks how the face is presented, not how many dogs there are.
parsed.missing_data: A separate comparison of frontal pose with averted gaze against frontal pose with direct gaze, plus non-dog frontal faces (cats, humans), would show whether eye contact or frontal pose drives the unit and whether it is specific to dogs.

real_s1.explanation: The unit responds to a dog's face seen frontally with both eyes open and looking at the camera, and it is strongest when the head is large in the frame.

parsed.explanation: The unit responds to a dog's face seen frontally with both eyes open and looking at the camera, and it is strongest when the head is large in the frame.
parsed.evidence: The eye-visibility, frontal-gaze and head-size predictions all held (d +1.64, +1.28, +1.18; percentiles 99, 97, 96). The portrait-vs-whole-body prediction was weaker (d +0.56, percentile 84), which suggests the unit tracks visible frontal eyes and face size rather than photo framing as such.
parsed.missing_data: Controlled comparisons that hold head size fixed and vary only gaze direction (frontal vs. turned), plus tests on non-dog frontal faces such as cats or humans, to tell whether the unit is dog-specific.

real_s3.explanation: The unit responds to a dog's face seen head-on and level, with the muzzle pointing at the camera and the eyes meeting the viewer, regardless of breed.

parsed.explanation: The unit responds to a dog's face seen head-on and level, with the muzzle pointing at the camera and the eyes meeting the viewer, regardless of breed.
parsed.evidence: Three predictions held: frontal vs. profile heads (d +1.24, 97th percentile), eye contact vs. looking elsewhere (d +0.88, 99th) and level vs. tilted heads (d +0.58, 97th) all separate activity strongly. The single-dog vs. multiple-dog contrast did not hold (73rd percentile, only 8 multi-dog photos), so the number of dogs is not shown to matter beyond the face geometry.
parsed.missing_data: Photos of frontal faces of non-dog animals or people with eye contact, to test whether the unit is specific to dogs, plus more multi-dog photos to settle the effect of dog count.

null_s1.explanation: Among its top dog-breed classes, the unit responds most to dogs whose faces are not engaging the camera: heads turned to profile or away, eyes hidden or not visible, and heads that are small in the frame. It is not a frontal eye-contact detector.

parsed.explanation: Among its top dog-breed classes, the unit responds most to dogs whose faces are not engaging the camera: heads turned to profile or away, eyes hidden or not visible, and heads that are small in the frame. It is not a frontal eye-contact detector.
parsed.evidence: Three predictions came out reversed. Activity was lower for frontal eye contact (d -0.42), large heads (d -0.42) and both eyes visible (d -0.71), which puts this unit among the lowest 4-5% of its layer on each, while the portrait-versus-whole-body question gave only a weak reversal (d -0.19, percentile 27).
parsed.missing_data: Activations on new photos split by head angle and dog size separately, to tell whether turned-away heads or small, distant dogs drive the unit, and to check that non-dog content isn't contributing.
